source.title: Compute Optimal Inference and Provable Amortisation Gap in Sparse Autoencoders

record.tranche_reason: The study uses sparse autoencoders to extract and assess features in GPT-2, but does not measure whether network neurons have unrelated mixed responses.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses superposition and reports comparisons of sparse-inference methods. Its GPT-2 interpretability evaluation concerns learned SAE, MLP, and LCA features, not polysemanticity of the network's own neurons or whether their mixed responses share a feature. Those adjacent interpretability results are recorded under fits_no_version; synthetic sparse-inference results are not rows for this claim.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAE/MLP/LCA dictionary learning on GPT-2 residual-stream activations and reports interpretability of the learned features. It never measures polysemanticity of the network's own neurons. Its synthetic results concern sparse-inference accuracy, not neuron behaviour in trained models.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors prove that linear-nonlinear SAE encoders have a non-zero amortisation gap. They show that sparse coding, and sometimes MLPs, beat SAEs on synthetic data. They also find MLP-encoder features on GPT-2 more interpretable than SAE/LCA features, at higher compute cost. They do not measure neuron polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares sparse inference and feature-extraction methods; it does not apply the original source's neuron-inspection method to test polysemanticity.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that interpretability scores differ by feature-extraction method; it does not test how polysemanticity measurements vary with activation range or scoring choices.

fits_no_version.finding: On GPT-2 Small layer 9 residual activations, MLP-encoder dictionary features scored higher automated-interpretability F1 (about 0.83) than SAE (about 0.63) and LCA (about 0.61) features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More expressive sparse encoders yield more interpretable dictionary features than linear-nonlinear SAEs.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy dictionary learning, SAE and MLP decoders showed large off-diagonal D^T D entries even when N matched the true dimension, which the authors read as superposition. The effect diminished with decoder normalisation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Learned SAE dictionaries can exhibit superposition-like feature overlap without capacity pressure.

record.problems: The interpretability result is an automated F1-based proxy, not a direct test of neuron polysemanticity. The paper notes that its LCA implementation was not optimized for the experiment and that it examined only top activations in its interpretability analysis.
record.rows_left_out: Synthetic sparse-inference and dictionary-learning results (Sections 4 and Appendices B–H) do not measure neuron polysemanticity or the behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models is measured.
Superposition appears only as background and as toy decoder-weight overlap (App. E). Neuron polysemanticity is never linked to it.
Initialization, regularization and noise as causes are not tested.
The share of polysemantic neurons across architectures or activations is not measured.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Activation-range dependence is only suggested as future work for SAE features. It is not tested on neurons.

record.verdict_notes: The Appendix E toy result (SAE dictionaries overlapping when N equals the true dimension) loosely resembles V4. However, it concerns SAE decoder columns in synthetic data, not neurons of a trained network, so it is listed under fits_no_version with no linked rows. The Figure 7 annotations (μ, N=2500) are inconsistent with the text (500 features, medians).

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or neuron responses to image inputs are examined.
No share of polysemantic MLP neurons or unrelated language-model contexts is measured.
The paper discusses superposition, but does not test whether it causes neuron polysemanticity through capacity pressure.
Initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemantic neurons are not tested.
Encoder methods are compared on feature interpretability, but the share of polysemantic neurons and its relation to architecture, activation, regularization, or performance is not measured.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
The study does not compare activation-range choices or explanation-scoring choices as measurements of neuron polysemanticity.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small Layer 9 SAE feature set
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated automated feature explanations against held-out activation examples using F1.

conditions.value: residual-stream pre-activations at Layer 9 of GPT-2 Small

rows.note: This evaluates explanations of learned SAE features, not polysemanticity of GPT-2 neurons.
rows.check: The measure is the interpretability of learned SAE dictionary features, not of GPT-2 neurons. Figure 7 shows a mean of 0.63 with N=2500, while the text says 500 features and a median around 0.6.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Small Layer 9 SAE, MLP, and LCA feature sets
rows.operation_detail: Compared F1-score distributions across the three feature-extraction methods using statistical tests.

conditions.value: residual-stream pre-activations at Layer 9 of GPT-2 Small

rows.measure: Kruskal-Wallis test of interpretability F1 distributions
rows.baseline: Comparison among SAE, MLP, and LCA
rows.value: H = 1856.33, p < 0.001; Dunn’s tests with Bonferroni correction found SAE and LCA significantly below MLP (p < 0.001)
rows.note: Statistical differences concern automated feature-interpretability scores, not neuron polysemanticity.
rows.check: This is a comparison of the study's own methods (encoder variants) on feature interpretability, not a measure of the claim's behaviour.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
